526.title: I am he (John 18:1–11)
526.hook: the soldiers fall back at his words
526.howItsDone: The arrest in the garden opens the Passion according to John, which Catholics hear on Good Friday; on Holy Thursday night, some parishes keep a watch of prayer after the evening Mass, remembering the garden.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ecumenism, and the prayer that closed the supper: that they all may be one.

A garden at night, across a small valley from the city walls. Olive trees, the smell of crushed leaves, and down the slope a line of lights coming up: torches and lanterns, a detachment of soldiers, officers from the chief priests, the glint of weapons. Leading them is someone who knows exactly where to find this garden, because Jesus often met his disciples here. It's Judas. A chase in the dark would be the obvious next scene. John tells it very differently.
screen: `A GARDEN ACROSS THE KIDRON.` → `TORCHES COMING UP THE SLOPE.` → `JUDAS KNOWS THE PLACE.`

segments.voice: John says Jesus knew all that was coming upon him, and he went forth. He doesn't wait to be found. He walks out to meet them and asks, whom seek ye? Jesus of Nazareth, they say. And he answers with two words, in Greek egō eimi, which the Douay-Rheims renders: "I am he." Then John adds this: "As soon therefore as he had said to them: I am he; they went backward, and fell to the ground." Armed men, with torches, fall over. John doesn't explain it. But the reader has been hearing egō eimi all through this Gospel: I am the bread of life, I am the light of the world, and once, startlingly, before Abraham was made, I am. In the scriptures, I am is how God names himself to Moses at the burning bush. So when Jesus says it in the garden, John lets the words land with weight, and the arresting party ends up on the ground. He asks again, whom seek ye, and gets the same answer. Then: if you seek me, let these go their way. He trades himself for his friends, the good shepherd in a single sentence. Peter draws a sword and cuts off the right ear of the high priest's servant, and John gives us the servant's name: Malchus. Jesus stops him: put up thy sword into the scabbard. He isn't trapped here. He's choosing. And it all begins with saying, plainly, who he is.

Then picture one place where you tend to hide who you are, or what you believe, or what you did, and see yourself there simply answering, that's me. If you pray, hold Jesus's words, I am he, and ask for courage; if you don't, just stand and breathe.

527.title: What is truth, again (John 18:33–38)
527.hook: my kingdom is not of this world
527.howItsDone: Catholics hear this exchange every Good Friday, when the Passion according to John is read or sung, often with several voices taking the parts of the narrator, Jesus, Pilate and the crowd.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the garden, and soldiers falling back at two words. Your line was put up thy sword.

Early in the morning, John says, the accusers bring Jesus to the governor's palace, then stop at the door. It's the Passover, and they won't go in, so they won't be defiled before the feast. So Pilate has to keep crossing the threshold: out to the crowd, in to the prisoner, out again. John builds the whole trial that way, scene by scene, outside and inside. Pilate's famous question came up early on this path. This time, stay inside the room: a prisoner and a governor alone, and the sentence that started it.
screen: `THE ACCUSERS STOP AT THE DOOR.` → `PILATE GOES IN AND OUT.` → `A PRISONER AND A GOVERNOR.`

segments.voice: Pilate asks: art thou the king of the Jews? For Rome, that's the only question. A king is a rival to Caesar. Jesus answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "My kingdom is not of this world." It's easy to hear that as: my kingdom is somewhere far away, nothing to do with here. But the Greek says ek tou kosmou, out of this world, from it. He's talking about where his kingdom comes from, not where it isn't. It doesn't grow out of armies and taxes and fear. And he proves it on the spot: if it were that kind of kingdom, his servants would be fighting. A few hours ago, Peter tried, and Jesus told him to put the sword away. Pilate grabs the word: so you are a king? And Jesus says, "For this was I born, and for this came I into the world; that I should give testimony to the truth. Every one that is of the truth, heareth my voice." This king doesn't command by force. His people are the ones who hear his voice: the good shepherd again, sheep who know the voice. Then Pilate asks, what is truth, and walks back out to the crowd without waiting for an answer. Look at the two men. One keeps crossing a doorway, trying to satisfy the people outside and Caesar far away. The other stands still. A kingdom not from this world isn't a kingdom with nothing to say to this world. It means a loyalty that no flag, party or boss handed out, so none of them gets the whole person.

528.title: Behold the man (John 19:1–5)
528.hook: crowned with thorns and shown to the crowd
528.howItsDone: Catholics meditate on the crowning with thorns in the third Sorrowful Mystery of the rosary, and on Jesus's condemnation at the first Station of the Cross.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a king whose kingdom is not from here. Your line was not of this world.

Two Latin words label a scene that painters kept coming back to. A man with his hands bound, a crown of thorns, a red or purple cloak hanging off his shoulders, sometimes a reed in his hand like a fake scepter. Next to him, a man in fine clothes, pointing. Below, faces in a crowd. Titian painted it. So did Caravaggio. It hangs in churches and galleries, one version after another. Those two words come from today's few verses.
screen: `ONE SCENE, PAINTED AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `THORNS, A CLOAK, A POINTING HAND.` → `TWO LATIN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Pilate has found no case against Jesus. He offers to release him, and the crowd outside calls for Barabbas instead. So Pilate has him scourged. Then the soldiers turn it into a game. They plait a crown out of thorns and press it on his head. They throw a purple garment over him, a mock king's robe, and come up to him again and again saying, hail, king of the Jews, and strike him. Then Pilate walks him out in front of the crowd. In the Douay-Rheims: "Jesus therefore came forth, bearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment. And he saith to them: Behold the Man." In Latin, Ecce homo. What did Pilate mean? Maybe, look at him, he's harmless, he's had enough. Maybe contempt. John doesn't say. But Christians have heard more in it than Pilate meant. Behold the man: not just this man, but what a human being looks like when he has been mocked and stripped of everything, and still is who he is. The Church sees there, too, the servant Isaiah described, in the Douay: "Despised, and the most abject of men." That's part of why painters kept coming back to it. It asks the viewer to do what Pilate asked the crowd: look, and don't look away. Look at the man in the purple rag and see a person, a king even, in the one everyone is laughing at.

529.title: Woman, behold thy son (John 19:25–27)
529.hook: the disciple takes her into his own home; Catholics hear Mary given to all
529.carry: he took her to his own
529.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of the Church, on the Monday after Pentecost, and some keep an image of Mary at home and pray the Hail Mary each day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ecce homo: the mocked man shown to the crowd. Your line was look with compassion.

People in hospice often spend their last strength on the people they're leaving. Who'll take care of Mom? Make sure your sister's okay. Promise me you'll call him. When everything else is slipping away, what's left is love, arranging things. Jesus has been nailed to a cross outside Jerusalem, and the soldiers are dividing his clothes at the foot of it. John notices who else is standing there, close enough to hear. A few women. One disciple. And his mother.
screen: `LAST STRENGTH, FOR OTHERS.` → `SOLDIERS DIVIDE HIS CLOTHES.` → `AND HIS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: John names them: his mother, his mother's sister, Mary of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene. And the disciple whom Jesus loved, never named in this Gospel, whom tradition identifies as John. Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "When Jesus therefore had seen his mother and the disciple standing whom he loved, he saith to his mother: Woman, behold thy son. After that, he saith to the disciple: Behold thy mother. And from that hour, the disciple took her to his own." Woman. It sounds cold in English. It wasn't, then; it was a respectful way to address a woman. But it's an unusual word for a son to use with his mother, and John has had Jesus use it with her before. At the wedding in Cana, at the very start, Jesus said to her: woman, what is that to me and to thee? My hour is not yet come. Now the hour has come, and he says woman again. The two scenes are bookends. Some readers also hear an echo of the first woman in Genesis, the mother of all the living. On one level, this is a dying son making sure his mother isn't left alone. But Catholics have heard more. The disciple stands for every disciple, so Mary is given as mother to all who follow Jesus. Pope Paul the Sixth named her Mother of the Church during the Second Vatican Council, and Pope Francis later gave that title its own memorial, on the Monday after Pentecost. Some Christians, especially Protestants, read the scene mainly as a son's care for his mother. And from that hour, the text says, he took her to his own.

530.title: Blood and water (John 19:31–37)
530.hook: a soldier pierces his side; the Fathers saw baptism and the Eucharist flow out
530.howItsDone: Catholics honor the pierced heart of Jesus on the Solemnity of the Sacred Heart, and some pray before the Divine Mercy image, whose two rays stand for the blood and water.

segments.voice: Yesterday, woman, behold thy son: Mary given to the beloved disciple. Your line was he took her to his own.

There's a detail on many crucifixes that's easy to walk past: a wound in the right side, under the ribs. Sometimes it's just a red line. Some old paintings show a thin stream running from it, caught in a cup by an angel. In the Divine Mercy image, two rays, one pale and one red, pour out from that same place. All of it comes from a single moment, after Jesus has already died, that John says an eyewitness swore to.
screen: `A WOUND IN THE SIDE.` → `TWO RAYS, PALE AND RED.` → `ONE MOMENT AFTER DEATH.`

segments.voice: It's Friday, the day of preparation, and the sabbath about to begin is, John says, a great sabbath day. The authorities don't want bodies on crosses over the holy day, so they ask Pilate to have the legs broken to hasten death. The soldiers break the legs of the two men crucified with Jesus. When they come to him, he's already dead. Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "But one of the soldiers with a spear opened his side, and immediately there came out blood and water." John stops the story to swear to it: the one who saw it has given testimony, and his testimony is true, so that you also may believe. Why does it matter so much? Partly, it shows he was truly dead, against anyone who'd say otherwise. Partly, John sees scripture fulfilled: not a bone of him shall be broken, as with the Passover lamb, and from Zechariah, "They shall look on him whom they pierced." But the early Church saw more. Notice the Douay's word, opened, which follows the Latin. Saint Augustine noticed it too. He wrote that the evangelist chose the word opened because there the door of life was opened, from which the sacraments of the Church flowed out: water for baptism, blood for the Eucharist. Some of the Fathers added a picture from Genesis: as Eve was formed from the side of the sleeping Adam, the Church was born from the side of Christ asleep on the cross. The Catechism repeats that image. That's why Catholics look so carefully at that wound.

531.title: Apostle to the apostles (John 20:11–18)
531.hook: Mary Magdalene is sent to tell the others; Pope Francis raised her day to a feast in 2016
531.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Feast of Saint Mary Magdalene on July 22, with the Gloria at Mass and her encounter with the risen Jesus read as the Gospel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, blood and water from the opened side. Your line was they shall look on him.

Early Sunday morning, still dark. Mary Magdalene has come to the tomb and found the stone rolled away. She ran for Peter and the beloved disciple. They came running, saw the linen cloths lying there, and went home. She didn't. She's standing outside the tomb, crying. It's the kind of crying where you can't leave, because leaving would make it real. Everyone else has gone. And she's the one who stays.
screen: `THE STONE ROLLED AWAY.` → `THE MEN GO HOME.` → `SHE STAYS, CRYING.`

segments.voice: She stoops to look into the tomb and sees two angels where the body had been. Woman, why weepest thou? Because they have taken away my Lord, she says, and I know not where they have laid him. She turns and sees a man she takes for the gardener. Sir, if you've carried him off, tell me where, and I'll take him away. Then he says one word. In the Douay-Rheims: "Jesus saith to her: Mary. She turning, saith to him: Rabboni (which is to say, Master)." Not a speech. Her name. The good shepherd said his sheep know his voice when he calls them by name, and here it happens. Then Jesus says, do not touch me, for I am not yet ascended. The Latin, noli me tangere, gave its name to many paintings. The Greek may mean something closer to, don't hold on to me, don't cling. Because she has a job. Go to my brethren, he says, and tell them. And she does. The text says: Mary Magdalen cometh and telleth the disciples, "I have seen the Lord," and what he said to her. In John's telling, she's the one sent with the news, sent to the apostles themselves. Christian writers came to give her a title for it: apostle to the apostles. Apostle means one who is sent. In 2016 Pope Francis raised her day, July 22, from a memorial to a feast, the same rank as the feasts of the apostles, and the decree used that old title.

532.title: Receive ye the Holy Ghost (John 20:19–23)
532.hook: he breathes on them: whose sins you forgive; the Church roots confession here
532.howItsDone: Catholics confess their sins to a priest in the sacrament of penance; the priest prays the words of absolution, which name the Holy Spirit sent for the forgiveness of sins, and sends the penitent away in peace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary Magdalene, apostle to the apostles. Your line was I have seen the lord.

Sunday evening, the same day. Mary has told them what she saw. And the disciples are in a room with the doors shut, John says, for fear: men who ran away three days ago, jumping at every footstep on the stairs, wondering if they're next, wondering what they'll say if he really is alive. Not a room full of faith. A room full of nerves and guilt. And then he's simply there, standing in the middle of them. His first words are today's line.
screen: `DOORS SHUT, FOR FEAR.` → `MEN WHO RAN AWAY.` → `HE STANDS IN THE MIDST.`

segments.voice: He says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Peace be to you." No accusation. No, where were you? He shows them his hands and his side, the opened side from two days ago, and they're glad. Then he says it again, peace be to you, and adds: as the Father hath sent me, I also send you. And John records something strange and physical: "he breathed on them; and he said to them: Receive ye the Holy Ghost. Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them: and whose sins you shall retain, they are retained." That word, breathed, is rare in the Greek Bible. In the Greek translation of Genesis, the same verb is used when God breathes the breath of life into the first human. Here, on the first day of a new week, Jesus breathes again, and many readers, ancient and modern, hear a new creation beginning. And the first thing the breath is for is forgiveness. Remember who's in the room: men who denied him and ran. The first gift given to them is the power to forgive. The Catholic Church roots the sacrament of penance, confession, in this moment. The Council of Trent taught that here Christ gave the apostles and their successors the power to forgive and retain sins, and the Catechism cites this verse. That's why, in confession, the priest's words of absolution speak of the Holy Spirit sent among us for the forgiveness of sins, and of pardon and peace. And that's week seventy-six: I am he, not of this world, Ecce Homo, woman, blood and water, the apostle to the apostles, and the breath of peace.
screen: `PEACE BE TO YOU.` · `AS THE FATHER SENT ME.` · `HE BREATHED ON THEM.` · `THE ROOT OF CONFESSION.` · then, large: `RECEIVE YE THE HOLY GHOST.`

segments.voice: Let your breath slow down by itself, cool coming in, warm going out. If there's something you feel guilty about today, let it be in the room with you, the way the disciples' failures were, and don't argue with it: on each in-breath, receive peace; on each out-breath, let a little of the fear go. If you pray, hold Jesus's first words, peace be to you; if you don't, just breathe.
Breathed. The rare word for what the risen Jesus did to his frightened disciples, echoing the breath of life in Genesis, before sending them to forgive. Today's word.
Your line: peace be to you. Not an accusation came first, but peace. Day five hundred thirty-two.
screen: `WEEK SEVENTY-SIX: EGŌ EIMI · NOT OF THIS WORLD · ECCE HOMO · WOMAN · BLOOD AND WATER · APOSTLE · BREATH`
